name: Daria Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a plant that makes plastic parts for medical kit, mostly syringe barrels and the little caps on inhalers. I gown up, go into the clean room and look after four injection moulding machines, which melt plastic pellets and squirt them into moulds. My day is checking parts under the light, swapping moulds when we change product, and logging everything, because if a batch is wrong it could end up in a hospital. I like that it matters, and I like my line lead, Priya, but twelve-hour shifts in a hairnet get old fast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside work right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who drives buses, and we're renting a flat above a bakery on Mill Lane. We've got about ten months of expenses put aside, plus a separate pot for a house deposit we've been building for four years. I'm careful, but I'm not tight, and we still go out on a Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably laugh and say, well, that was a lot of fuss over nothing. Priya would say she knew it all along, because she says that about everything. Online I'd maybe share a funny meme and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd be a relief, because it means Sam and I can stick to the plan: buy a place in a year or two, keep my job, maybe start a family later. I've used one of those chat assistants a few times, mostly to help word a complaint to our landlord, and that's about as far as AI has got in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. Keep putting money in the deposit pot every month and keep chatting to people at work about joining a union, because we haven't got one and we should. Nothing about AI being a flop changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bit flat, like when a storm warning comes to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned wanting a union. Why does that matter to you if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because things go wrong even without robots. Last year they changed our shift pattern with a week's notice and nobody could say no. If AI turns out to be nothing, the management is still the thing that ruins your weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets the first bit of money if things just carry on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house, no question. We've looked at a two-bedroom near the park three times now, and I'd want to put in an offer before prices climb again.

S0.say: I'd laugh and say it was a lot of fuss over nothing. I'd share a meme online and get back to normal life.
S0.think: Honestly, it'd be a relief, because it keeps our plan on track: buy a place soon, keep my job and maybe start a family later. AI has barely touched my life beyond wording a letter.
S0.do: Keeps working and paying into the house deposit pot every month. Keeps talking to colleagues about forming a union, and would put in an offer on a two-bedroom near the park.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sense of anticlimax.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be nothing, the management is still the thing that ruins your weekend.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is a planner with a clear life script: house, then maybe children. Even in the calmest picture she brings up the lack of a union, which says she worries more about management than about machines. She treats AI as something she's dabbled in, not something she relies on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a union now, before the changes start, not after. I'd share articles about other factories that got a fair deal. I'd also say I'm not against the technology, I just want a say in how it comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the moulding machines themselves are already pretty automatic, so the bit that's at risk is me: the checking and the mould changes. That's what a camera and a robot arm would do. I've seen videos of it already at other plants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Priya whether the company has plans and push hard to get us organised. I'd also start using those AI assistants a bit more, like for the paperwork and batch logs, because if that's where things are going I'd rather not be last. And I'd still buy the house, but maybe a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching the managers' faces in every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy the house, but cheaper. Why cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a mortgage feels different if you're not sure your job looks the same in three years. I'd want to be able to pay it on Sam's wage alone if I had to. That's my rule, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a man called Dev on nights who only does the visual checks. Dev's eyes are the whole job, and I've seen cameras that never blink doing that same job. I'd want the union to fight for him first.

S1.say: I'd say this is why we need a union now, before the changes start. I'm not against the technology, I just want workers to have a say in how it comes in.
S1.think: I think the machines are already automatic, so the checking and the mould changes are the parts of my job at risk. I've already seen cameras and robot arms doing that at other plants.
S1.do: Pushes harder to organise a union and asks her line lead about company plans. Starts using AI tools more for batch logs and paperwork, and still buys a home but a cheaper one.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful, without real fear yet.
S1.quote: Dev's eyes are the whole job, and I've seen cameras that never blink doing that same job.
S1.fieldNote: Daria combines collective action with a modest personal adjustment, which is very much the steady profile. Her rule that the mortgage must be payable on one wage shows careful thinking. She worries first about a colleague whose job is pure visual checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, letting a handful of companies switch this on before anyone is ready. I'd be calling for the government to slow it down and make the companies pay for whatever comes next. I'd be at the protests with Sam, he'd bring a flask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job's gone within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. The clean room is perfect for robots, it's tidy, it's the same thing over and over. I'm only twenty-seven, so I don't even have the excuse of being nearly done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house hunt straight away and sit on the deposit as savings. I'd join whatever union or workers' group would have us, even a general one. And I'd sit down with Sam and work out how long we could last on his wage, because buses might hold out a bit longer than factories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three in the morning, which is ridiculous, because we'd be fine for a while on the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have two years' warning. Would you try to learn anything new in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, but I don't know what. Two years isn't enough to become a nurse, and anyway the card says it can do almost anything. I think I'd spend the two years organising and saving, and figure out the rest once I see what's actually left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house plans, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four years of saving for a deposit, and I'd end up treating it like a life raft instead of a front door. We'd keep renting above the bakery. I'd hate it, but I wouldn't sign a mortgage with my job about to vanish.

S2.say: I'd say it's reckless to let a handful of companies switch this on before anyone is ready. The government should slow it down and make the companies pay for what comes next.
S2.think: I think my clean-room job would be gone within a year, because it's perfect work for robots. I'm only twenty-seven, so I've got far too much working life left to shrug it off.
S2.do: Stops house hunting and keeps the deposit as an emergency fund. Joins any union or workers' group she can and plans with Sam how long they could live on his wage alone.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, though she knows the money would hold for a while.
S2.quote: Four years of saving for a deposit, and I'd end up treating it like a life raft instead of a front door.
S2.fieldNote: The sharpest loss for Daria is the house plan, not the money itself. Two years feels too short for her to pick a new path, so she defaults to organising and saving. She notes the irony of panicking while being financially secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd be telling everyone to organise now, while we still have a bit of power to bargain. I'd post about countries or companies doing it well, if there were any. And I'd be telling the managers I want the training before the robots show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough time to do something with myself, and that changes how I feel. I could do a course in maintenance, the people who fix the robots, and maybe that buys me a few more years. It might not last forever, but it's better than sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening course in automation maintenance at the college on Station Road, about two nights a week. I'd keep saving and keep the deposit untouched for now. I'd push for the union, obviously, and try to get the company to pay for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Like having a deadline at school, you know it's coming but you can plan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the maintenance work might not last forever either. Why bother, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because three extra years of a good wage is three more years of saving, and that's real. And honestly, I'd rather be the person who knows how the new machines work. Being useful feels better than being pushed aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide about the house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until I'd finished the course and seen whether the company kept me on. If they did, maybe we'd buy something small around year three. If they didn't, at least the deposit would still be sitting there doing its job as a safety net.

S3.say: I'd tell everyone to organise now while workers still have some bargaining power. I'd tell my managers I want training before the robots arrive.
S3.think: Five years is enough time to do something useful with myself. A maintenance course could buy me a few more years of good pay, even if it doesn't last forever.
S3.do: Signs up for a two-nights-a-week automation maintenance course at the local college in the first year, asking the company to pay. Keeps saving, keeps the deposit untouched and keeps pushing for a union.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, like a school deadline she can plan for.
S3.quote: If they didn't, at least the deposit would still be sitting there doing its job as a safety net.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years move Daria from defence to a concrete plan, a maintenance course. She is clear-eyed that it buys time rather than security. The house decision is now tied to whether the course pays off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so let's use them properly: training paid for by the companies, a shorter working week, and a proper safety net. I'd be one of the people organising at my plant. I'd probably sound a bit like a broken record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it feel like a career change rather than an emergency. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. That's young enough to move into something else and still have it count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course in the first year and then look for a job in robot maintenance at a bigger plant, maybe in year two or three. We'd buy the house, a small one, around year two, and I'd keep putting a bit aside every month. I'd also start using the AI tools regularly, because by then everyone will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the others. I'd have time to be the one who changes, not the one who gets changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the medical plant to do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, yes. I'd miss Priya and the clean room, weirdly, but staying loyal to a machine that's about to replace you is a bit daft. I'd go where the robot work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change your thoughts about starting a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want to be settled in the new job first, so maybe we'd wait until I was thirty or so. Sam would be fine with that, he's in no hurry.

S4.say: I'd say we have ten years, so let's use them for company-paid training, a shorter working week and a proper safety net. I'd organise at my plant.
S4.think: Ten years makes it feel like a career change rather than an emergency. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which is young enough to make a new path count.
S4.do: Takes the maintenance course in the first year and looks for robot maintenance work at a bigger plant within two or three years. Buys a small home around year two and starts using AI tools regularly.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, feeling she can be the one who changes.
S4.quote: staying loyal to a machine that's about to replace you is a bit daft.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Daria becomes the most forward-looking she's been, willing to leave a workplace she likes. Her family plans shift a little but don't collapse. The steady pattern shows: she moves once she can see a proven path.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to change anything except my bank balance. I can handle hard work, what I can't handle is being told it's over before I've had a chance to try something else. What would help is paid training, before the robots arrive, and a union so we're not just told what's happening by email.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it'd affect people who are just starting a family. Everyone talks about older workers, which is fair, but people my age are making big decisions right now, houses and kids, and this stuff hangs over all of it.

headlineQuote: I can handle hard work, what I can't handle is being told it's over before I've had a chance to try something else.
portrait: Daria is a 27-year-old injection moulding operator in a medical plastics clean room, living with her bus-driver partner Sam and saving hard for a first home. She's careful with money, likes her work because it matters, and has been quietly pushing for a union. She moves from calm in the plateau to alarmed when AGI is two years away, mostly because it would freeze her house and family plans. Given five or ten years she plans a maintenance course and a move to robot maintenance work, showing she'll change once she can see a proven path.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to change anything and she'd be told it's over before she could try something new.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training before the robots arrive, and a union so workers aren't just told what's happening by email.
